findings.message: The `HaveDifferentTypes` / `HasDifferentType` function in the Maglev graph builder uses `IntersectType(lhs_type, rhs_type) == NodeType::kUnknown` (i.e., bitwise AND == 0) to decide that two value-nodes must have different runtime types. This heuristic is semantically incorrect: two NodeTypes can share no bit flags yet still admit a common concrete subtype. The canonical example is `kAnyHeapObject` (bit 5 only, value 32) and `kNumber` (bits 3-1, value 14): their bitwise AND is 0, so the old code declares them disjoint and short-circuits `lhs === rhs` to `false`. However, `kHeapNumber` (= `kAnyHeapObject | kNumber` = 46) is a valid subtype of both, so the same HeapNumber could appear on both sides. When a phi or type-widened node has type `kAnyHeapObject` on one side and a numerically-typed node has type `kNumber` on the other, `BuildTaggedEqual` incorrectly returns the constant `false`, producing a result that diverges from the interpreter and triggers the correctness fuzzer.
findings.suggestion: Replace the bitwise-AND-zero test with a semantic disjointness check. Rather than checking whether the type bits have no overlap (IntersectType == 0), combine the two types with OR (CombineType = bitwise OR) and then test whether the resulting combined type is provably uninhabited according to a curated list of mutually-exclusive property pairs. This is what the fix commit does: it introduces `NodeTypeCannotHaveInstances(CombineType(lhs_type, rhs_type))` with the exclusive-pairs list `{AnyHeapObject,Smi}, {NumberOrOddball,Name}, {NumberOrOddball,JSReceiver}, {JSReceiver,Name}`. Because `CombineType(kAnyHeapObject, kNumber)` equals `kHeapNumber`, which does not appear in any exclusive pair, the two types are correctly recognized as non-disjoint and the `===` fold is not applied.
findings.title: Incorrect type-disjointness check via bitwise AND causes wrong `===` folding in Maglev

ground_truth.root_cause: The disjointness predicate confused structural bit-disjointness (no shared flag bits) with logical type-disjointness (no common inhabitant). The NodeType lattice deliberately shares certain bits only along subtype edges, so two types can have no common bits yet share a common concrete subtype (e.g., `kHeapNumber ⊂ kAnyHeapObject` and `kHeapNumber ⊂ kNumber`). Using bitwise AND to test disjointness is only correct when every pair of disjoint concrete types also has disjoint bit representations, which the lattice does not guarantee.

commit_message:
[Merged] [wasm] Share import wrappers per WasmEngine

IOW, share them per process, instead of duplicating them for each
NativeModule. Detailed changes:

- The WasmImportWrapperCache is promoted from having an instance per
  NativeModule to having an instance per WasmEngine. It also gets its
  own code space for storing wrappers.
- Wrapper compilation functions now return a WasmCompilationResult
  instead of an already-published WasmCode, so that callers can decide
  where to put the WasmCode. That is done, specifically, by the
  WasmImportWrapperCache.
- WasmCode objects used for wrappers now don't have a NativeModule,
  i.e. their native_module_ == nullptr.
- Whereas wrappers previously had their lifetime implicitly tied to the
  NativeModule that owned them, we must now accurately track their
  refcount.
- To this end, WasmDispatchTables get an off-heap WasmDispatchTableData,
  which keeps track of all wrappers referenced by the table. Storing
  this information off-heap is necessary so that it's still available
  when the table's finalizer is invoked (at which time the table itself
  can no longer be accessed).

Using shared wrappers for WasmJSFunctions is left for a future patch.

pr_description:
Share compiled Wasm import wrappers across NativeModules through a process-wide cache with its own code space. Track wrapper references in off-heap dispatch-table data so their lifetime remains independent of any single NativeModule.

Track entry into code collection with an atomic dying flag on each WasmCode. Cache lookups hold scoped references and decline dying wrappers, while dispatch-table installation checks that wrappers remain eligible for use. Stack lookups retain visibility of dying code until its remaining activations finish, and the engine no longer needs a separate dead-code set.

findings.message: WasmImportWrapperCache::MaybeGet() increments the reference count of a cached WasmCode wrapper via WasmCodeRefScope::AddRef() and returns the pointer without checking whether the code object is already in the dying state (i.e., has been added to the WasmEngine's potentially_dead_code_ or dead_code_ sets). A racing Wasm Code GC cycle can have already decremented the code's reference count to zero and placed it on the dead_wrappers list for immediate freeing via WasmImportWrapperCache::Free(). The resurrection — incrementing the ref count from the lookup — does not stop the GC from calling FreeDeadCodeLocked, which erases the entry from the cache, frees the JIT code allocation, and calls 'delete wrapper'. The caller of MaybeGet() is left holding a dangling WasmCode pointer whose underlying JIT memory has been reclaimed, leading to a use-after-free that can corrupt JIT-allocated memory. The same class of defect exists in CompileWasmImportCallWrapper (which returns a cached wrapper from cache_scope[key] without an is_dying check) and FindWrapper (which returns a pointer without even adding a ref guard).

related_locations.description: Returns a cached dying wrapper without checking is_dying(): 'wasm_code = cache_scope[key]; if (wasm_code) return wasm_code;'
Returns a pointer to a potentially-dead code object without adding a ref guard or checking is_dying()
The resurrection guard checks dead_code_.contains(code) but does NOT mark the code on the WasmCode object itself; the cache has no way to detect the dying state without a per-object flag
Moves code from potentially_dead_code_ to dead_code_, calls DecRefOnDeadCode(), then frees via FreeDeadCodeLocked — racing with concurrent MaybeGet callers

findings.suggestion: Before returning a wrapper from any cache lookup, check whether the code object is already marked as dying. Add an atomic 'is_dying_' bit to WasmCode and set it the first time the code is added to potentially_dead_code_ in AddPotentiallyDeadCode. All cache lookup paths (MaybeGet, CompileWasmImportCallWrapper, FindWrapper) must check this bit — under the cache lock, after AddRef — and return nullptr if the code is dying, forcing the caller to compile a fresh wrapper instead.

ground_truth.root_cause: Commit a5999be introduced a shared, process-wide WasmImportWrapperCache with independent reference counting for wrapper WasmCode objects. The cache lookup functions (MaybeGet, and later FindWrapper/CompileWasmImportCallWrapper) were written to return cached pointers after incrementing the ref count, but without any mechanism to detect that the code had already entered the GC dying path. The engine-level dead_code_ set tracked dying wrappers but was not accessible from the cache's lookup hot-path under the cache lock. Without a per-object dying flag visible to the cache, there was no way for lookups to detect the race and refuse to return a doomed pointer.

findings.message: TypeCanonicalizer::LookupStruct, LookupArray, and LookupFunctionSignature are called with untrusted canonical type indices sourced from sandboxed WebAssembly bytecode. After a range-bounds check (SBXCHECK), the code retrieves the CanonicalType* and then verifies its kind with DCHECK_EQ. Because DCHECK_EQ compiles to a no-op in release (non-debug) builds, an attacker who can supply an in-bounds type index that refers to a different type kind (e.g., an array-type index passed to LookupStruct) will bypass the kind check entirely. The function then reads the wrong union member (e.g., type->struct_type when the actual union payload is array_type or function_sig), resulting in a type-confused pointer being returned to the caller and ultimately allowing a V8 sandbox violation via the subsequent StructTypeBase::field access.
findings.suggestion: Replace DCHECK_EQ(type->kind, CanonicalType::kStruct) (and the equivalent checks in LookupArray and LookupFunctionSignature) with SBXCHECK(type->kind == CanonicalType::kStruct). SBXCHECK is enforced in both debug and release builds and terminates the process on failure, preventing the type-confused pointer from being returned.

commit_message:
[Merged] [string] Optimize and refactor index hashing

gotos are considered harmful and switches are not, so extract out
helper functions from index hashing which report whether the index
contained non-index (non-digit or leading zero) values, or whether it
simply overflowed.

Also do some microoptimisation that merges the index check with the
conversion to decimal, and changes the overflow check to detect overflow
(with a single branch) rather than prevent it (with branches dependent
on both the current digit and the value so far). This should reduce
branches and tighten the loop.

gotos are considered harmful and switches are not, so extract out
helper functions from index hashing which report whether the index
contained non-index (non-digit or leading zero) values, or whether it
simply overflowed.

Also do some microoptimisation that merges the index check with the
conversion to decimal, and changes the overflow check to detect overflow
(with a single branch) rather than prevent it (with branches dependent
on both the current digit and the value so far). This should reduce
branches and tighten the loop.

findings.message: In `TryParseArrayIndex`, the `index` accumulator is declared as `uint32_t`. For 10-digit strings on 64-bit platforms, the loop expression `index = (10 * index) + val` can silently overflow a 32-bit integer. After the full loop, an overflow-detection block attempts to undo the last iteration via `index -= chars[i - 1]`. This undo is doubly wrong: (1) it subtracts the raw ASCII character value (e.g., 50 for '2') rather than the digit numeric value (e.g., 2), and (2) it does not account for the wrapping that occurred in the multiplication `10 * index`, which destroys information and is not reversible. As a concrete example, parsing '8589934640' causes `10 * 858993464 + 0 = 8589934640` to wrap to 48 (mod 2^32). The undo then computes `48 - '0' = 48 - 48 = 0`. When this corrupted zero is passed to `TryParseIntegerIndex`, the assertion `DCHECK_GT(index, 0)` at line 183 fires, crashing a debug build.

related_locations.description: DCHECK_GT(index, 0) fires when the corrupted (zero) index is passed in after the flawed undo
uint32_t& index parameter declaration — the root cause of the overflow on 64-bit platforms

findings.suggestion: Use a 64-bit accumulator on 64-bit platforms so the multiplication never overflows for values in the valid integer-index range. The fix introduces `using ArrayIndexT = uint64_t` on 64-bit hosts and `uint32_t` on 32-bit hosts, then uses `ArrayIndexT& index` throughout. On 64-bit, overflow detection reduces to a simple `if (index > String::kMaxArrayIndex) return kOverflow;` without any undo logic.
findings.title: uint32_t overflow with unrecoverable undo in TryParseArrayIndex

ground_truth.root_cause: The `index` variable was typed as `uint32_t` even on 64-bit platforms where integer indices can legitimately exceed 32-bit range before the overflow boundary is reached. When `10 * index` wraps a 32-bit integer, information is permanently lost; the subsequent subtraction-based undo cannot reconstruct the original value. The overflow detection condition (`index + 1 < kMinValidValue + 1`) also fails to catch all overflow cases where the wrapped result accidentally falls within the valid uint32_t range.

findings.message: In `FastJsonStringifier::SerializeObject`, when a JSObject or JSArray is encountered, the code unconditionally calls `obj->map()->map()->native_context()` to retrieve the native context. However, for detached globals (and other objects with context-less meta maps), the meta-map is the read-only `meta_map` root, which has no associated native context. Calling `native_context()` on it triggers a DCHECK failure (`IsNativeContext(*this)`) in `contexts-inl.h`. This was introduced when the fast-path check was refactored to front-load prototype comparisons: the new code obtained the native context early in `SerializeObject` without guarding against context-less meta maps. A malicious page can trigger this via `JSON.stringify` on a detached cross-realm global, causing a crash in debug builds and undefined behavior in release builds.
findings.suggestion: Before calling `native_context()` on the meta-map, check whether it is the context-less read-only `meta_map` root. If it is, bail out to the slow path rather than attempting to dereference a non-existent native context. This is exactly what the fix commit does.

The refactored code assumed every JSObject/JSArray would have a meta-map with a native context, which is false for detached globals whose meta-map is the read-only `meta_map` root. No guard was added to handle this case before invoking `native_context()`.

findings.message: In `LastIndexOfValueImpl`, a special-case branch introduced to handle 0 == -0 semantics for Float16Array (where both +0 and -0 share different bit patterns) returns early using `start_from` as a raw array index without first re-checking the current array length. The `start_from` value is computed by the JavaScript engine from the caller-supplied `fromIndex` argument via `ToInteger`, which can invoke user-defined `valueOf()` methods. If such a method shrinks the backing resizable ArrayBuffer (RAB) — e.g., via `ab.resize(0)` — then `start_from` can exceed the new array length. The early-exit do-while loop then computes `data_ptr + k` where `k >= typed_array_length`, constituting an out-of-bounds read on the underlying backing store. The general code path (for other element types or non-zero search values) is protected by a post-conversion bounds adjustment block that re-reads `typed_array->GetLength()` and clamps `start_from` accordingly, but the Float16 zero special case short-circuits before reaching that guard.

related_locations.description: The bounds re-check that is bypassed: re-reads typed_array_length and clamps start_from after potential side effects from ToTypedSearchValue/ToInteger
Regression test demonstrating the exploit: valueOf() resizes the RAB to 0 while lastIndexOf(0, evil) computes fromIndex

findings.suggestion: Move the Float16 zero-equality check inside the main loop that runs after the `start_from >= typed_array_length` bounds adjustment. Use `if constexpr (IsFloat16TypedArrayElementsKind(Kind))` inside the loop body so the check is compiled away for non-Float16 element kinds, preserving performance while ensuring `start_from` has already been clamped to the current (possibly shrunk) array length before the loop begins.

findings.message: In `Typer::Visitor::ObjectIsArrayBufferView`, after a parent commit changed `TypeJSCreateTypedArray` to return `Type::TypedArray()` instead of `Type::OtherObject()`, commit 65beb80d9cd added an early true-return for pure TypedArray inputs but failed to update the false-return guard on the next line. The condition `!type.Maybe(Type::OtherObject())` is still checked to decide whether to return `singleton_false_`. Because typed arrays are now typed as `TypedArray` (not `OtherObject`) in the type lattice, a union type like `TypedArray | Boolean` satisfies `!type.Maybe(Type::OtherObject())` (neither TypedArray nor Boolean overlaps OtherObject), so the function incorrectly returns `singleton_false_` — asserting that the value *cannot* be an ArrayBufferView even when it is a typed array. This incorrect type annotation creates a type contradiction in Turbofan's incremental type-propagation loop, triggering a FATAL assertion at line 451 (`UpdateType error`) when the propagated type widens unexpectedly.
findings.suggestion: Change the false-return guard from `Type::OtherObject()` to `Type::TypedArray()` so that any type that could possibly be a TypedArray is not prematurely ruled out as a non-ArrayBufferView.

findings.message: In `NodeProperties::InferMapsUnsafe`, the newly introduced `case IrOpcode::kTransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap` only updates `*maps_out` and returns when `receiver` and `object` are identical via `IsSame()`. When they are not identical (the `else` path), it silently `break`s without setting `result = kUnreliableMaps`. Because `receiver` and `object` may still alias at runtime (pointing to the same heap object through different SSA paths/phi nodes), the `TransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap` operation can change the receiver's map even when `IsSame()` returns false. Callers of `InferMapsUnsafe` then receive stale/incorrect map information and proceed with optimizations that assume an impossible type, triggering a SIGTRAP (debug assertion) in the compiled code.
findings.suggestion: Before the `break` in the `kTransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap` case, add `result = kUnreliableMaps;` to indicate that any previously inferred maps for the receiver are no longer reliable, because the aliasing object's map may have been transitioned.
findings.title: Missing kUnreliableMaps in TransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap case of InferMapsUnsafe

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Missing kUnreliableMaps in TransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap case of InferMapsUnsafe
Related location for: Missing kUnreliableMaps in TransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap case of InferMapsUnsafe
Related location for: Missing kUnreliableMaps in TransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap case of InferMapsUnsafe

ground_truth.root_cause: The new `kTransitionElementsKindOrCheckMap` case in `InferMapsUnsafe` only considers the trivial aliasing case (`IsSame`). It neglects the possibility of non-trivial aliasing (same heap object reachable via different SSA value paths). Other opcodes in the same function that can have side effects on aliasing objects correctly set `result = kUnreliableMaps` before breaking; the new case was missing this defensive assignment.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix d3e1723bf45a on top of intro 3e7191831b1a via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError):  Root cause: When AsmJs opcodes were moved to a new prefix (0xfa) in the refactoring commit 3e7191831b, the new DecodeAsmJsOpcode function was written with V8_ASSUME to assert the opcode prefix rather than validating it. The read_prefixed_opcode function uses LEB128 decoding for the opcode index byte, so a multi-byte LEB128 value (index > 0xFF) produces an opcode with a different bit layout than expected by the ASSUME assertion. The original author assumed V8_ASSUME was a mere optimizer hint, not realizing it also embeds a hard DCHECK in debug builds.

findings.message: The function DecodeAsmJsOpcode uses V8_ASSUME((opcode >> 8) == kAsmJsPrefix) instead of a proper validation check. V8_ASSUME expands to a DCHECK in debug builds, causing a crash when an invalid AsmJs opcode reaches this function. The vulnerability is triggered via read_prefixed_opcode which uses LEB128 decoding: if the attacker supplies the AsmJs prefix byte (0xfa) followed by a LEB128-encoded index > 0xFF but <= 0xFFF, read_prefixed_opcode constructs the opcode as (*pc << 12 | index), whose high 8 bits do NOT equal kAsmJsPrefix (0xfa), violating the DCHECK. Similarly, if the LEB128 index > 0xFFF in validation mode, read_prefixed_opcode returns kExprUnreachable (0), which also fails the check. In release builds, V8_ASSUME with a false condition is undefined behavior for the optimizer, potentially enabling security exploitation. A crafted AsmJS wasm module can reliably trigger this crash.
findings.suggestion: Replace V8_ASSUME with an explicit guard check that calls DecodeError and returns 0 when (opcode >> 8) != kAsmJsPrefix. This ensures malformed bytecode is rejected gracefully rather than triggering an assertion or undefined behavior.
findings.title: Missing guard in DecodeAsmJsOpcode allows invalid opcode to trigger DCHECK crash

ground_truth.root_cause: When AsmJs opcodes were moved to a new prefix (0xfa) in the refactoring commit 3e7191831b, the new DecodeAsmJsOpcode function was written with V8_ASSUME to assert the opcode prefix rather than validating it. The read_prefixed_opcode function uses LEB128 decoding for the opcode index byte, so a multi-byte LEB128 value (index > 0xFF) produces an opcode with a different bit layout than expected by the ASSUME assertion. The original author assumed V8_ASSUME was a mere optimizer hint, not realizing it also embeds a hard DCHECK in debug builds.

findings.message: When building the map cache (mode == kBuildingMapCache), the ResumeJSObject function incorrectly uses `descriptor_idx` directly as `property_index` instead of `details.field_index()`. The optimization of using the descriptor number as the field index is only valid for the fast-map-cache case (kWithMapCache), where all properties are guaranteed to be consecutive, enumerable, and stored as in-object fields in descriptor order. For kBuildingMapCache mode, the map is not yet validated as fast, so property field indices can differ from their descriptor indices. This causes a DCHECK failure in debug builds and incorrect property slot access in release builds, potentially reading the wrong property value or accessing memory out of the intended object layout.
findings.suggestion: Move the `int property_index` declaration inside the conditional branches so that the non-fast (kBuildingMapCache / kWithoutMapCache) branch assigns `property_index = details.field_index()` and only the kWithMapCache branch assigns `property_index = descriptor_idx`. This matches the fix applied in ba4aa40.

agent_reasoning: Lazy page allocation removes the assumption that allocation failure means new space has reached its target capacity. Without checking capacity, allocation failures caused by resource exhaustion could enter AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity with its invariants violated. ReachedTargetCapacity compares the active semispace's current capacity against the target, and EnsureAllocation returns false when allocation fails below that target, preserving the beyond-capacity path's preconditions. Changes are limited to the two source files from the supplied correction; no tests were modified.
commit_message:
[Merged] [heap] Grow new space lazily to target capacity

So far SemiSpaceNewSpace was always eagerly allocating pages to reach
its target capacity (for both semi spaces). This CL relaxes this
and allocates pages lazily when they are needed for allocation.

This improves bomb-workers by about 0.8%.

fix_commit_message:
[heap] Add early bailout on allocation slow path for new space

So far it was always the case that we reached
AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity only if the space has already reached
its target capacity. However, now that we lazily allocate new space
pages allocation can also fail when the current capacity is below
the target capacity. E.g. because we run out of virtual memory in
the cage or other OOM situations. This now starts to triggger the
DCHECKs in AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity, which assume that the
space is full. Instead of removing these DCHECKs this CL fixes this
by adding an early bailout in EnsureAllocation(). With this we
only invoke ShouldExpandYoungGenerationOnSlowAllocation() for the
SemiSpaceNewSpace if the space is actually at its capacity.

findings.message: After the lazy new-space page allocation was introduced, `SemiSpaceNewSpaceAllocatorPolicy::EnsureAllocation()` can reach the `AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity()` call even when `to_space_` has not yet grown to its `target_capacity_`. `AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity()` contains two DCHECKs that assume the space is already full: `DCHECK_LT(Available(), size_in_bytes)` and `DCHECK(!AddFreshPage())`. When allocation fails due to OOM or virtual-memory exhaustion before the space reaches its target capacity, `Available()` returns `target_capacity_` (because `Capacity() = max(current_capacity_, target_capacity_) = target_capacity_` while `Size() ≈ 0`), which is far larger than `size_in_bytes`, causing the first DCHECK to fire.

related_locations.description: DCHECK_LT(Available(), size_in_bytes) — the DCHECK that fires when the space has not reached target capacity
Capacity() returns max(current_capacity_, target_capacity_), so Available() equals full target_capacity_ when no pages have been lazily allocated yet

findings.suggestion: Before deciding to call ShouldExpandYoungGenerationOnSlowAllocation() (and subsequently AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity()), check whether the space has actually reached its target capacity. If it has not, bail out early and return false, because the failure was caused by an OOM/virtual-memory shortage, not by the space simply being full. The fix adds a ReachedTargetCapacity() predicate (to_space_.current_capacity_ >= target_capacity_) and gates the expansion path on it.

ground_truth.root_cause: The lazy page allocation feature removed the invariant that 'allocation failure ⇒ space is at target capacity.' The `EnsureAllocation()` function on the slow path did not add a guard to verify `to_space_.current_capacity_ >= target_capacity_` before entering the beyond-capacity code path. As a result, `AllocateOnNewPageBeyondCapacity()` is reached in states it was never designed to handle, where `Available()` equals the full target capacity rather than a value smaller than the requested allocation size.

findings.message: When regular wasm functions emit a SetStackPointer instruction (added to support central stack switching for Fast API calls), the SP is temporarily invalidated. The ARM64 code generator has an optimization in SlotToMemOperand() that converts FP-relative slot offsets to SP-relative memory operands when the encoding is more efficient. This optimization is gated by FPRelativeOnly(), but the SetFPRelativeOnly(true) call in AssembleCode() (src/compiler/backend/code-generator.cc) only covers WASM_TO_JS_FUNCTION code kind, kWasmToJsWrapperCSA, and wasm builtins — NOT regular WASM_FUNCTION code. As a result, after this commit introduced SetStackPointer into regular wasm Fast API call paths, the generated ARM64 code could use SP-relative operands during a window where the SP points to the central stack, causing accesses to the wrong memory region and triggering the 'metadata->Chunk() == this' CHECK failure in the heap.
findings.suggestion: The FPRelativeOnly guard must cover all code that may emit a SetStackPointer instruction, including regular WASM_FUNCTION code. The fix replaces the coarse-grained code-kind check with precise detection: during instruction selection, when a SetStackPointer opcode is encountered, set an 'invalidates_sp' flag on the Frame object. Then in the ARM64 operand converter, check frame()->invalidates_sp() instead of FPRelativeOnly(). This ensures any function that actually performs a stack switch — regardless of code kind — disables the SP-relative operand optimization for its entire compilation.

findings.message: In `FastJsonStringifier::ResumeJSObject`, after completing the descriptor loop the code unconditionally promotes the DescriptorArray's fast-iterable state from `kUnknown` to `kJsonFast`. However, `nof_descriptors` is derived from `map->NumberOfOwnDescriptors()`, which may be less than `descriptors->number_of_descriptors()` because DescriptorArrays are shared among maps in the same map-tree (e.g. a parent map and a child map that adds more properties share the same DescriptorArray prefix). When only a prefix of the DescriptorArray has been validated, marking the entire array as `kJsonFast` is incorrect. On a subsequent `JSON.stringify` call for an object that shares the same DescriptorArray but has more own properties, `ResumeJSObject` is entered in `kJsonFast` mode and the code assumes `descriptor_idx == field_index` (the DCHECK at line 2774) without re-validating the never-iterated tail descriptors. That assumption is false, producing a DCHECK crash in debug builds and silent wrong-property reads in release builds.
findings.suggestion: Only update the DescriptorArray to `kJsonFast` if all descriptors in the array were actually iterated, i.e. guard the promotion with `if (nof_descriptors == descriptors->number_of_descriptors())`. This matches the fix in commit 7a68d07.

agent_reasoning: The original C call opcodes fell outside IsCallWithDescriptorFlags and used the opcode misc field for parameter counts, preventing fast API calls from carrying kHasExceptionHandler. Moving ArchCallCFunction into the descriptor-aware opcode range and placing parameter counts in a separate input preserves exception and frame-state flags. All nine backends consume the separate counts and register handler and deoptimization metadata according to those flags, eliminating the dedicated frame-state opcode. Changes are scoped to the 12 source files touched by the supplied correction; no test files were edited.
commit_message:
[Merged] [fastcall] Support throwing exceptions

A function called with a fast call can set a flag on the isolate to
indicate that an exception has been thrown. As for normally throwing an
exception, the exception has to be stored on the isolate anyways.
Generated code then checks after a fast call if the flag on the isolate
is set. If so, a runtime function is called that triggers stack
unwinding through the normal exception handling of the C-Entry stub.

Additionally deopt info is added to fast API calls, not because deopt is
possible, but because deopt info is needed to generate stack traces for
exceptions.

The CL does the following changes:
(1) The TurboFan node `FastApiCall` gets two control outputs for
`IfSuccess` and `IfException`;
(2) The Turboshaft operation `FastApiCallOp` gets the ability to throw
an exception, and gets a FrameState input so that deopt information is
generated for the call;
(3) The instruction selector adds to a `kArchCallCFunction` the
information if deopt info is needed for the call, and the code generator
generates deopt info in that case;
(4) A new flag is added to the isolate that allows generated code to
check after a fast API call whether an exception has been thrown.

R=dmercadier@chromium.org

fix_commit_message:
[compiler] Encode param counts of C calls as extra input

In the instruction sequence, CallDescriptor flags typically get encoded
in the misc field of the opcode for calls. C Calls, however, did not
need the CallDescriptor flags and instead encoded the parameter count in
the misc field.

For fast API calls, however, the CallDescriptor flags are needed.
With this CL, the CallDescriptor flags now gets encoded in the misc
field also for C calls. The parameter count gets passed in an additional
input.

findings.message: The introducing commit added kArchCallCFunctionWithFrameState to distinguish fast API calls that need deopt/frame-state info, but placed both kArchCallCFunction and kArchCallCFunctionWithFrameState AFTER kArchCallBuiltinPointer in the opcode enum. IsCallWithDescriptorFlags() is implemented as 'arch_opcode <= kArchCallBuiltinPointer', so both CFunction opcodes fall outside that predicate. As a result, HasCallDescriptorFlag() always fires a DCHECK for CFunction instructions, and the MiscField in those opcodes is occupied by ParamField/FPParamField (parameter counts) instead of CallDescriptor::flags. When a fast API call carries kHasExceptionHandler (i.e., it can throw), VisitCall never encodes that flag into the opcode and the code generators (e.g., code-generator-x64.cc) never register an exception handler for the call site. When such a call actually throws an exception, the missing handler causes an unexpected trap inside Builtins_InterpreterEntryTrampoline.
findings.suggestion: Move kArchCallCFunction into the IsCallWithDescriptorFlags opcode range (before kArchCallBuiltinPointer). Remove the separate kArchCallCFunctionWithFrameState opcode. Encode param counts as an extra instruction input operand (not in the MiscField), and use EncodeCallDescriptorFlags(kArchCallCFunction, flags) so that kHasExceptionHandler, kNeedsFrameState, and other CallDescriptor flags are properly stored and queryable via HasCallDescriptorFlag() in every architecture's code generator.

ground_truth.root_cause: The introducing commit added kArchCallCFunctionWithFrameState after kArchCallBuiltinPointer in the COMMON_ARCH_OPCODE_LIST macro. The IsCallWithDescriptorFlags() predicate is a simple range check ('arch_opcode <= kArchCallBuiltinPointer'), so both CFunction opcodes are excluded. Consequently, the MiscField—which must carry CallDescriptor::flags for calls inside that range—was instead used to store the GP and FP parameter counts. With no way to encode kHasExceptionHandler, the code generators never set up exception handlers for fast API call sites.

pr_description:
A function called with a fast call can set a flag on the isolate to
indicate that an exception has been thrown. As for normally throwing an
exception, the exception has to be stored on the isolate anyways.
Generated code then checks after a fast call if the flag on the isolate
is set. If so, a runtime function is called that triggers stack
unwinding through the normal exception handling of the C-Entry stub.

Additionally deopt info is added to fast API calls, not because deopt is
possible, but because deopt info is needed to generate stack traces for
exceptions.

The CL does the following changes:
(1) The TurboFan node `FastApiCall` gets two control outputs for
`IfSuccess` and `IfException`;
(2) The Turboshaft operation `FastApiCallOp` gets the ability to throw
an exception, and gets a FrameState input so that deopt information is
generated for the call;
(3) The instruction selector adds to a `kArchCallCFunction` the
information if deopt info is needed for the call, and the code generator
generates deopt info in that case;
(4) A new flag is added to the isolate that allows generated code to
check after a fast API call whether an exception has been thrown.

findings.message: In KnownMapsMerger::IntersectWithKnownNodeAspects, when all possible maps for an object are filtered out during intersection (intersect_set_ becomes empty), the commit changed node_type_ from NodeType::kUnknown to EmptyNodeType(). This is semantically correct, but BuildCheckMaps did not add a corresponding guard to detect when the combined type (CombineType(merger.node_type(), GetType(object))) becomes empty — an impossible/dead state. When known_maps_are_subset_of_requested_maps_ is true but the intersect set is empty (maps were filtered by IsInstanceOfNodeType), BuildCheckMaps enters the 'done' branch, calls known_info->IntersectType(EmptyNodeType()), sets the node's type to the empty type, and returns Done without emitting a deopt. Subsequent code generation over this logically-dead graph node proceeds to emit stores via BuildStoreTaggedFieldNoWriteBarrier, which asserts DCHECK(CanElideWriteBarrier(object, value)). Because the object's type is now the empty/impossible type the assertion fails, producing the reported DCHECK crash.
findings.suggestion: After calling merger.IntersectWithKnownNodeAspects in BuildCheckMaps, check whether the resulting combined type is empty (impossible). If so, emit an unconditional deopt immediately — before reaching the known_maps_are_subset_of_requested_maps() branch — so that no dead code with inconsistent type assumptions is generated. The same guard should be applied in TryBuildPolymorphicPropertyAccess for the SMI-path selection.

findings.message: In `TryBuildStoreField`, when the field representation is double and the access has a transition map, the code calls `GetAccumulator()` to obtain `float64_value` without first checking whether the accumulator's node type is empty (which signals unreachable/dead code in the Maglev type system). The empty-typed value is then wrapped in a `Float64ToHeapNumberForField` node and passed to `BuildStoreTaggedField`. Inside `BuildStoreTaggedField`, `CanElideWriteBarrier` is called on the resulting tagged heap-number node. Because the write-barrier logic cannot consistently determine whether a barrier is needed for a value derived from dead-code (empty-type) operands, a DCHECK failure is triggered. The type system refactoring (commit 7556d7f) changed `NodeTypeIs` semantics so that the empty type is a mathematical subset of every type (via bit-mask arithmetic), enabling values with empty types to propagate silently through type checks that previously rejected them. A partial fix (commit 6953465) guarded `CanElideWriteBarrier` itself but left a TODO acknowledging that `TryBuildStoreField` still needed an early bailout for empty-typed values.
findings.suggestion: Before entering the double-field handling block (and indeed before all type-specific checks in TryBuildStoreField), retrieve the accumulator value once and immediately bail out with an unconditional deopt when its node type is empty. This matches the fix applied in the fix commit: move `value = GetAccumulator()` to before the double block and insert `if (IsEmptyNodeType(GetType(value))) return EmitUnconditionalDeopt(DeoptimizeReason::kWrongValue);`.

findings.message: In `RegExpMatchGlobalAtom_OneCharPattern`, the SIMD-optimized implementation stores its match count with an assignment `*number_of_matches = matches` rather than accumulation `*number_of_matches += matches`. The caller (`RegExpMatchGlobalAtom`) first calls `RegExpResultsCache_MatchGlobalAtom::TryGet` which, on a cache hit, pre-populates `number_of_matches` with the previously cached count before invoking the dispatch function. The assignment inside the SIMD path silently discards this cached count and replaces it with only the new (incremental) count. The corrupted value (which can be 0 when no additional matches exist beyond the cached position) is then stored back into the cache via `TryInsert`. On the next call with the same subject/pattern, `TryGet` retrieves the corrupted cache entry with `number_of_matches == 0`, immediately triggering the `DCHECK_GT(number_of_matches, 0)` assertion in the caller.
findings.suggestion: Change the assignment to accumulation so that matches found in a prior (cached) invocation are preserved. The caller passes in the already-populated `number_of_matches` from a cache hit and expects the SIMD path to add onto it, not replace it.
findings.title: Match count overwritten instead of accumulated in SIMD regexp path

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Match count overwritten instead of accumulated in SIMD regexp path
Related location for: Match count overwritten instead of accumulated in SIMD regexp path

ground_truth.root_cause: The original scalar loop incremented `*number_of_matches` in-place (`(*number_of_matches)++`), naturally accumulating across any prior cached value. The SIMD rewrite introduced a local `int matches = 0` accumulator for vectorized counting efficiency, but the final store was written as assignment (`*number_of_matches = matches`) rather than as accumulation (`*number_of_matches += matches`), breaking the API contract that the output pointer is an in-out parameter when called after a cache hit.

findings.message: In Uint8ArrayToBase64 (later renamed Uint8ArrayPrototypeToBase64), the expression `uint8array->GetBuffer()->backing_store()` is called inside a `DisallowGarbageCollection no_gc;` scope. `GetBuffer()` returns a Handle<JSArrayBuffer> which may require heap allocation to materialize the JSArrayBuffer object. Performing such an allocation while GC is explicitly disallowed triggers a V8 DCHECK failure: `AllowGarbageCollection::IsAllowed()` in heap.cc. The fix is to use `uint8array->DataPtr()`, which directly returns the raw data pointer of the typed array without any heap allocation.
findings.suggestion: Replace `uint8array->GetBuffer()->backing_store()` with `uint8array->DataPtr()`. The DataPtr() accessor returns the typed array's data pointer directly as a raw pointer without performing any heap allocation, making it safe to call inside a DisallowGarbageCollection scope.

findings.message: In `VisitSpeculativeAdditiveOp`, the refactored condition `BothInputsAre(node, Type::Signed32())` is too narrow: it does not cover inputs whose type is `Unsigned32` (but not `Signed32`). The original code handled both signed and unsigned 32-bit integer inputs through the `kAdditiveSafeIntegerOrMinusZero` check (which includes the full integral32 range). With the narrowed guard, a node whose inputs are `Unsigned32` no longer enters the fast Int32Add/Sub path. Instead it falls through to a different lowering path. This produces a mismatch in `UseInfo` between the PROPAGATE and LOWER phases: the two phases assign different `UseInfo` values for the same input edge, violating the monotonicity invariant checked by `DCHECK(IsUseLessGeneral(input_use_infos_[index], use_info))` in simplified-lowering.cc, causing a crash (a DCHECK failure that in a non-debug build could silently produce incorrect code).
findings.suggestion: Replace `BothInputsAre(node, Type::Signed32())` with `BothInputsAre(node, Type::Integral32OrMinusZero())` so that both `Signed32` and `Unsigned32` inputs enter the Int32Add/Sub fast path, preserving the pre-existing monotonic UseInfo invariant across compiler phases.

findings.message: In `Uint8ArrayPrototypeSetFromHex`, after checking for out-of-bounds and detached conditions, the code proceeds to call `uint8array->DataPtr()` without first checking whether `array_length == 0`. For a zero-length `Uint8Array` (e.g., one backed by a zero-length `SharedArrayBuffer`), `DataPtr()` returns `nullptr` because there is no backing memory. This null pointer is then passed directly as the output buffer argument to `ArrayBufferFromHex`. Even though `output_length` is clamped to 0 via `std::min(output_length, array_length)`, the `ArrayBufferFromHex` call (or the code path within it) still dereferences or processes the null pointer, triggering a crash.
findings.suggestion: Add an early-return check for `array_length == 0` immediately after the out-of-bounds/detached check and before the `output_length` computation and `DataPtr()` call. Return a result object with 0 bytes read and 0 bytes written.

findings.message: The newly-introduced `GetConstantSingleCharacterStringFromCode` function handles the two-byte (code > 255) case by calling `local_isolate()->factory()->LookupSingleCharacterStringFromCode(code)` and wrapping the result with `MakeRef(broker(), ...)`. A freshly-allocated two-byte single-character string created via the local isolate's factory does not satisfy these invariants, causing a CHECK failure in heap-refs.cc (`Ref construction failed`). This crash is reproducible whenever Maglev constant-folds a string element or `charAt` access that results in a two-byte (non-Latin-1) character, crashing the V8 engine process.
findings.suggestion: For two-byte (non-Latin-1) single-character strings, bail out of constant folding instead of attempting to wrap the factory-allocated string in a heap ref. Return an empty `MaybeReduceResult` (i.e., `{}`) for the two-byte path, as the ref construction infrastructure does not support this allocation pattern.

findings.message: The introducing commit `22f006269` added a `check_safe_integer_` field to the `Truncation` class and updated `IsLessGeneralThan()` to enforce `(check_safe_integer() <= other.check_safe_integer())` as part of the monotonicity check in Turbofan's simplified lowering pass. It correctly marked `CheckedSafeIntTruncatingWord32` with `Truncation::Word32WithSafeIntCheck()` (check_safe_integer=true), but left `CheckedSafeIntAsWord64` using the plain `Truncation::Any()` (check_safe_integer=false). When a JIT-compiled node is first visited with a use_info whose truncation carries check_safe_integer=true (e.g., via Generalize of a Word32WithSafeIntCheck truncation), and then revisited with `CheckedSafeIntAsWord64`'s `Truncation::Any()` (check_safe_integer=false), the monotonicity DCHECK `IsLessGeneralThan(true, false)` evaluates to false and fires: `DCHECK(IsUseLessGeneral(input_use_infos_[index], use_info))` in simplified-lowering.cc.
findings.suggestion: Use `Truncation::Any(kDistinguishZeros, true)` instead of `Truncation::Any()` in `CheckedSafeIntAsWord64` to set `check_safe_integer = true`, consistent with `CheckedSafeIntTruncatingWord32` using `Truncation::Word32WithSafeIntCheck()`. This ensures the monotonicity invariant holds when both UseInfo types are mixed during Turbofan's iterative re-processing of nodes.

findings.message: In the slow-path fallback of `ArrayBufferFromHex` in `src/objects/simd.cc`, the loop iterates `for (uint32_t i = 0; i < input_length; i += 2)`, where `input_length` is the full length of the hex input string. The output buffer is allocated with capacity `output_length` bytes (one byte per two hex digits). However, `DCHECK_LE(output_length, input_length / 2)` permits `output_length < input_length / 2`, meaning the input can contain more hex digit pairs than the buffer can hold. When this occurs, the loop continues writing decoded bytes via `buffer[index++] = result.value()` beyond the end of the allocated buffer, causing a heap buffer overflow. The SIMD fast paths (SSE/NEON) correctly bound their loops with `output_length * 2`, making only the scalar slow path vulnerable.
findings.suggestion: Change the loop upper bound from `input_length` to `output_length * 2` so the scalar slow path, like the SIMD fast paths, never writes more bytes than the buffer was allocated to hold.

findings.message: SLPTree::HasInputDependencies performs a BFS to verify that two nodes can safely be force-packed together (i.e., neither depends on the other). However, it has two critical omissions. First, it does not track 'reorder inputs': when a node has already been identified as an intermediate node in the BFS of a prior force-pack dependency check (across SLPTrees), that node may later itself be nominated for force-packing, breaking the assumption that nodes with smaller OpIndex will always be emitted before nodes with larger OpIndex. The commit introducing intersecting ForcePackNode created exactly this scenario, where a force-packing node from one SLPTree becomes an input of a force-packing node in another SLPTree that gets reduced earlier. Second, the BFS traversal does not check for side effects between intermediate nodes: even without a direct data-dependency path, if there are side-effecting operations between the BFS boundary and the candidate start node, reordering is unsafe. These two omissions cause NewForcePackNode and NewIntersectPackNode to create invalid force-pack pairings. At reduction time, ReduceForceOrIntersectPackNode then tries to emit out-of-order inputs using ReduceInputsOfOp, operating on nodes whose output mappings are not yet established, ultimately leading to a segfault in the generated JSToWasm wrapper trampoline.
findings.suggestion: Before the BFS, check whether either node in the group is already a tracked 'reorder input' (i.e., it appeared as an intermediate node during a prior HasInputDependencies call from a different SLPTree context). If so, return true immediately to reject the force-pack. Additionally, during the BFS, for each intermediate input between start and end, verify IsSideEffectFree(start_prev, input) — if any side effects exist, return true. After a successful BFS (returning false), merge all traversed intermediate nodes into the reorder_inputs_ set so they are excluded from future force-packing attempts.
findings.title: Incomplete dependency check allows unsafe force-packing of interdependent nodes

findings.message: In `ParseJsonObjectProperties<FastIterableState::kUnknown>()`, when the last key of a JSON object does not match the feedback descriptor (i.e., `is_slow || !key_match` is true) and no comma follows (i.e., it is the final property), the code falls through to `++idx` instead of returning. This incorrectly increments the descriptor index, making `idx == descriptors_end` true after the `do...while` loop exits. The subsequent check `if (idx == descriptors_end)` then calls `descriptors->set_fast_iterable_if(FastIterableState::kJsonFast, FastIterableState::kUnknown)`, marking the descriptor array as fast-iterable even though the last key failed to satisfy the fast-iterable requirements. This stale marking causes a DCHECK failure in `IsFastKey(obj, no_gc)` in `json-stringifier.cc` when the stringifier attempts to use the fast path on a descriptor array that was incorrectly promoted to `kJsonFast`.
findings.suggestion: Add `return true;` inside the `if (V8_UNLIKELY(is_slow || !key_match))` block, after the inner `if (Check(JsonToken::COMMA))` block, so that when no comma follows the mismatched last key the function returns immediately without executing `++idx` and without triggering the incorrect fast-iterable state promotion.

findings.message: In `BuildCallWithFeedback`, when the feedback target is a `FeedbackCell` (rather than a direct `JSFunction`), Maglev retrieves the `SharedFunctionInfo` and—if it is present—immediately proceeds to emit an inlined call via `TryBuildCallKnownJSFunction` without first checking whether the callee is a class constructor. Class constructors are non-callable: invoking one without `new` must throw a `TypeError`. Because the guard is absent, Maglev-optimized code silently executes the class body as if it were an ordinary function call, producing an incorrect result (no exception is thrown) instead of the spec-required `TypeError`. The fix adds `if (IsClassConstructor(shared->kind())) return BuildCallRuntime(Runtime::kThrowConstructorNonCallableError, {target_node});` before any inlining proceeds.

findings.message: The newly introduced TF_BUILTINs `AddRhsIsStringConstantInternalizeWithVector` and `AddRhsIsStringConstantInternalizeTrampoline` declare their parameters with swapped types: `left` is typed as `Parameter<String>` when it should be `Parameter<Object>` (since for the kRhsIsStringConstant variant, the left operand is an arbitrary value), and `right` is typed as `Parameter<Object>` when it should be `Parameter<String>` (since it is the constant string). This is a copy-paste error from the existing kLhsIsStringConstant builtin where the string IS on the left. The swapped types cause V8 to incorrectly treat any object passed as the left operand as a String type. When the left operand is a Growable SharedArrayBuffer (GSAB, i.e., `is_shared()=true && is_resizable_by_js()=true`), downstream code that calls `JSArrayBuffer::byte_length()` triggers the DCHECK `!is_shared() || !is_resizable_by_js()` in `src/objects/js-array-buffer-inl.h:36` because the GSAB object is incorrectly processed through string code paths.
findings.suggestion: Swap the parameter type declarations so that `left` is `Parameter<Object>` (arbitrary left operand) and `right` is `Parameter<String>` (the constant string on the rhs). This matches the calling convention for the kRhsIsStringConstant variant where only rhs is guaranteed to be a String.

findings.message: In `BuildCallWithFeedback`, when the feedback cell indicates a class constructor, `BuildCallRuntime(Runtime::kThrowConstructorNonCallableError, {target_node})` is invoked before `BuildCheckJSFunction(target_node)` or the feedback-cell reference check. This means `target_node` may not be a JSFunction at all when passed to `ThrowConstructorNonCallableError`. The runtime call internally casts its argument to `JSFunction`, triggering a DCHECK failure when the actual runtime value does not match that type (e.g., the slot was primed with a class constructor C1 but is subsequently called with a different non-JSFunction value).
findings.suggestion: Move the `IsClassConstructor` check to AFTER `BuildCheckJSFunction` and `BuildCheckValueByReference` so that `target_node` is guaranteed to be the expected JSFunction (with matching SFI and feedback cell) before it is passed to `ThrowConstructorNonCallableError`.
findings.title: ThrowConstructorNonCallableError called before validating target_node is a JSFunction

ground_truth.root_cause: The class-constructor early-return path was inserted BEFORE the `BuildCheckJSFunction` and `BuildCheckValueByReference` guards. Those guards normally deoptimize if `target_node` is not the expected JSFunction, but they are bypassed when the feedback indicates a class constructor. As a result, an arbitrary value can reach `ThrowConstructorNonCallableError`, which unconditionally treats it as a JSFunction.

agent_reasoning: Allocating the JavaScript ArrayBuffer inside the decoding helper would require allowing garbage collection while the caller still holds String::FlatContent under DisallowGarbageCollection. Collection could move the underlying string and violate FlatContent's lifetime invariant. The helper now returns native decoded storage and reports the decode result and output length; JavaScript allocation and copying happen only after FlatContent and its no-GC scope have ended. The edits retain the snapshot's Handle APIs and option variables while applying the supplied decoding and allocation changes.

[base64] Factor out AllowGC scope out of DisallowGC scope

This CL moves AllowGC scope out of DisallowGC scope to
make sure that FlatContent of the string is not moved
around by GC.

pr_description:
Add Uint8Array.fromBase64() with base64/base64url alphabets and configurable last-chunk handling. Decode the input into temporary native storage while garbage collection is disallowed, then allocate and populate the JavaScript ArrayBuffer after the string's FlatContent scope ends. Preserve syntax-error and out-of-memory reporting.

Validation: the candidate diff applies cleanly against the parent revision, and git diff --check passes.

findings.message: In BUILTIN(Uint8ArrayFromBase64), a DisallowGarbageCollection no_gc scope is created and String::FlatContent input_content is obtained from it (line 502). While this FlatContent is still live, ArrayBufferFromBase64() is called (lines 510-522), which internally creates an AllowGarbageCollection gc scope (line 399) and then calls isolate->factory()->NewJSArrayBufferAndBackingStore() — an operation that can trigger a GC cycle. When GC runs inside the AllowGarbageCollection scope, the heap-allocated input string may be moved or compacted. V8's slow-assert mode tracks a checksum of the string data at FlatContent construction time and re-verifies it at destruction time; after GC moves the string, the checksum no longer matches, causing the CHECK failure: `checksum_ == kChecksumValue`. The root cause is that the AllowGarbageCollection gc scope in the callee is inadvertently nested within the caller's DisallowGarbageCollection no_gc scope, violating the invariant that a String::FlatContent remains valid for its entire lifetime.
findings.suggestion: Move the AllowGarbageCollection scope and all heap allocations (NewJSArrayBufferAndBackingStore) out of the DisallowGarbageCollection scope. Perform all GC-safe string reads first, store results in a temporary buffer, destroy the DisallowGC scope and FlatContent, and only then allocate the JSArrayBuffer and memcpy the decoded data. This is exactly what the fix commit does: ArrayBufferFromBase64 is refactored to return std::unique_ptr<char[]> without any GC allocation, and the JSArrayBuffer allocation is moved to the caller after the DisallowGarbageCollection block closes.
findings.title: AllowGarbageCollection scope nested inside DisallowGarbageCollection invalidates live String::FlatContent

ground_truth.root_cause: The ArrayBufferFromBase64 helper was originally designed to both decode the base64 data AND allocate the output JSArrayBuffer in a single function. To allocate the JSArrayBuffer it needs AllowGarbageCollection, but the caller already holds a DisallowGarbageCollection scope (to safely read the String::FlatContent). Nesting AllowGarbageCollection inside DisallowGarbageCollection is forbidden by V8's invariants: a FlatContent is only guaranteed valid while GC cannot run, and allowing GC to run while the FlatContent is live can move the underlying string, breaking the checksum assertion on FlatContent destruction.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix ea0fdeca9749 on top of intro de42e588f4f7 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError):  Root cause: During the refactoring that introduced `GetVariableByteLengthOrOutOfBounds`, the old code naturally aligned the result by dividing by element size before returning (returning a count of elements). The new function returns byte length directly, but the author forgot to add the corresponding `RoundDown` to ensure the byte length is a valid multiple of the element size. The bug was latent because all prior callers divided the byte length by element size immediately after (so any partial byte at the end was silently truncated), but once byte length became the primary source of truth the misalignment became observable.

findings.message: In `GetVariableByteLengthOrOutOfBounds`, the byte length for length-tracking TypedArrays (both RAB-backed and GSAB-backed) is computed as the raw difference `buffer_byte_length - own_byte_offset` without rounding down to a multiple of the TypedArray's element size. When the buffer size is not evenly divisible by the element size (e.g., a 129-byte GSAB backing a Float64Array with 8-byte elements), the returned byte length (129) is not a valid multiple of the element size (should be 128). Any code that uses this byte length as the ground truth — such as checking `length * element_size == byte_length` — will encounter a DCHECK failure or incorrect behaviour, since 129 / 8 = 16 but 16 * 8 = 128 ≠ 129.
findings.suggestion: Round down the computed byte difference to the nearest multiple of the TypedArray's element size before returning. Use `RoundDown(buffer_byte_length - own_byte_offset, own_element_size)` for both the RAB and GSAB code paths, as the fix commit does.
findings.title: Missing element-size alignment when computing byte length for length-tracking TypedArrays

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Missing element-size alignment when computing byte length for length-tracking TypedArrays
Related location for: Missing element-size alignment when computing byte length for length-tracking TypedArrays

ground_truth.root_cause: During the refactoring that introduced `GetVariableByteLengthOrOutOfBounds`, the old code naturally aligned the result by dividing by element size before returning (returning a count of elements). The new function returns byte length directly, but the author forgot to add the corresponding `RoundDown` to ensure the byte length is a valid multiple of the element size. The bug was latent because all prior callers divided the byte length by element size immediately after (so any partial byte at the end was silently truncated), but once byte length became the primary source of truth the misalignment became observable.

findings.message: In `FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad()`, `last_continuation` and `after_continuation` are initialized to 0. The second switch iterates over CALL_PROPERTY_BYTECODES: the CASE macro only updates the variables when `iterator_.GetRegisterOperand(0) == loaded_property_register`. When the bytecode IS a CallProperty but the register does NOT match, the CASE executes `break` without updating the variables. The `default: return {}` only catches non-CallProperty bytecodes. The function then falls through to `return ContinuationOffsets{last_continuation, after_continuation}` which returns `{0, 0}` — a non-empty struct indicating a continuation was found at offset 0. The caller stores this as a valid continuation and later asserts `iterator_.current_offset() == continuation->last_continuation`, which fails because the iterator has advanced past offset 0.

related_locations.description: DCHECK site: asserts iterator_.current_offset() == continuation->last_continuation, which fires when continuation holds {0,0}

findings.suggestion: Return ContinuationOffsets immediately inside the CASE macro when a register match is found (early return), and change `default: return {}` to `default: break` so that non-CallProperty bytecodes also fall through to the final `return {}`. This ensures the function only returns a valid ContinuationOffsets when a genuine match is found, and always returns empty when no match is found.
findings.title: FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad returns invalid ContinuationOffsets{0,0} on register mismatch

However, `ContinuationOffsets{0, 0}` is structurally valid and is misinterpreted by the caller as a found continuation at offset 0. The `default: return {}` guard only protects against non-CallProperty bytecodes; a CallProperty bytecode with a mismatched register silently falls through to the final return with the zero-initialized values.

findings.message: In `FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad`, after each `iterator_.Advance()` call the code immediately inspects the current bytecode without checking whether the new offset is a merge point or loop header. When the pattern `GetNamedProperty -> Star -> CallProperty` straddles a loop back-edge or a merge point, the iterator is advanced into that merge-point offset and a continuation is returned for it. Later, when Maglev tries to generate the polymorphic call inline graph and jump into the middle of what the graph considers a loop/merge block, the block's state machine is in an invalid state, triggering the DCHECK `state_ == kBlockPointer` in `maglev-ir.h`.
findings.suggestion: After each `iterator_.Advance()` call in `FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad`, check whether the new offset is a merge point or loop header and return `{}` (no continuation) if so. Introduce a helper `IsOffsetAMergePointOrLoopHeader(int offset)` that combines `IsOffsetAMergePoint` and `bytecode_analysis().IsLoopHeader`.
findings.title: Missing merge-point/loop-header guard in FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad

ground_truth.root_cause: The function `FindContinuationForPolymorphicPropertyLoad` was introduced without the necessary guard that prevents it from identifying a continuation whose offsets land on bytecodes that are loop headers or merge points. Those offsets map to Maglev `MergePointInterpreterFrameState` objects that must be entered only via proper predecessor edges, not by jumping mid-continuation.

commit_message:
[Merged] [wasm] Support inlining Proxy-on-Prototype traps

When a Wasm object's prototype chain is sufficiently immutable,
we can statically retrieve Proxy traps on it and embed them as
constants. The existing Wasm-into-JS inlining support can then
even inline the calls, making keyed load/store accesses from
optimized code via these Proxy traps much faster.

findings.message: FeedbackNexus::IsOneMapManyNames() does not check the IC kind before classifying feedback as the '1 map, many names' type. This type is only valid for keyed load/store ICs, but the function can return true for KeyedHasIC feedback when the slot holds a Wasm object map with a generic handler. Commit ef9dafb5ab5 changed js-heap-broker.cc to call ProcessFeedbackMapsForKeyedPropertyAccess() whenever IsOneMapManyNames() returns true; that function contains DCHECK(keyed_mode.string_keys()). For KeyedHasIC, KeyedAccessMode::FromNexus() hard-codes string_keys=false (kStringKeysUnsupported), so the DCHECK fires and V8 crashes in debug builds.
findings.suggestion: Add an IC kind guard at the top of IsOneMapManyNames() to return false immediately for any IC that is not a keyed load or keyed store IC, since the '1 map, many names' feedback state is only produced by those two IC kinds.

findings.message: In `InsertUnreachableIfNecessary<LOWER>`, the ternary expression used to select a control node unconditionally calls `NodeProperties::GetControlInput(node, 0)` whenever `ControlOutputCount() == 0`. This assumes that any node without control outputs must have at least one control input. However, pure nodes (operator property `kPure`, e.g. `kSameValue`) have zero control inputs AND zero control outputs. When such a node produces a value of type `None` (e.g. through a type narrowing that makes the result impossible), the function is entered and `GetControlInput(node, 0)` triggers a CHECK failure in node-properties.h because `0 < node->op()->ControlInputCount()` is false (ControlInputCount is 0).
findings.suggestion: Before accessing the control input, check whether the node actually has control inputs. If the node has neither control inputs nor control outputs (i.e. it is a pure node), return early without inserting an Unreachable node, since there is no control edge to attach it to.
findings.title: Missing control-input guard in InsertUnreachableIfNecessary<LOWER> crashes on pure nodes

ground_truth.root_cause: The ternary guard `(node->op()->ControlOutputCount() == 0) ? GetControlInput(node, 0) : FindSuccessfulControlProjection(node)` only distinguishes between nodes with and without control outputs. It fails to handle the third case: pure nodes that have neither control inputs nor control outputs. This oversight was introduced when the function was refactored into a `<LOWER>` template specialization in 2020.

findings.message: In RepresentationSelector::VisitNode, when an effectful node (one with control/effect inputs) has a value input of type None (unreachable), the introducing commit changed the handling from properly disconnecting and replacing the node with a DeadValue to simply setting is_dead=true and returning after calling InsertUnreachableIfNecessary. InsertUnreachableIfNecessary only handles the effect chain by inserting an Unreachable node after the original node; it does not convert the original effectful node itself to a DeadValue. This leaves the effectful node in the graph as its original opcode but with feedback_type set to Type::None(). The LOWER phase returns without lowering the node, and when downstream code or the verifier later calls NodeProperties::GetType() on this untyped node, the DCHECK(IsTyped(node)) assertion fails. In release builds this inconsistency could lead to miscompilation of JIT-compiled JavaScript code.
findings.suggestion: For effectful nodes with control inputs (ControlInputCount() > 0) that have None-typed value inputs, create an Unreachable node using the node's effect and control inputs, redirect all effect/control uses of the original node to the new Unreachable, and convert the original node into a DeadValue. Do not rely on InsertUnreachableIfNecessary for this case as it does not convert the node itself. The condition guarding the dead-input detection also needs to be expanded to cover nodes with ControlInputCount() > 0 (effectful nodes without control outputs).

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 22e9d9621de5 on top of intro da0bcffa3d0c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError):  Root cause: The TDZ hole check elision optimization (`ignition_elide_redundant_tdz_checks`) added in `da0bcffa3d` placed `HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this)` at the start of `BuildOptionalChain`, covering the invocation of `expression_func()`. This function callback visits the actual chain expression, which may include TDZ variable accesses. The elision scope incorrectly treats all hole checks within the chain expression as redundant and suppresses them. The underlying assumption — that links 'earlier in the chain dominate later links' — applies to consecutive links of the same optional chain, but it incorrectly extends to the base object access itself, which is NOT dominated by any prior hole check.

findings.message: In `BuildOptionalChain`, a `HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this)` was placed unconditionally before `expression_func()` is called. This caused all Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) hole checks to be elided for any variable accessed as the BASE of an optional chain. When a TDZ variable (holding the internal sentinel TheHole) is the base of an optional chain, the expected `ThrowReferenceErrorIfHole` bytecode is not emitted. Because TheHole is not null/undefined, the subsequent `JumpIfUndefinedOrNull` optional chain check passes, allowing TheHole to propagate into JavaScript as if it were a real object. This bypasses the ECMAScript specification requirement that accessing an uninitialized binding throws a ReferenceError. The 'delete construct' variant specifically occurs when `delete tdz_var?.prop` is evaluated: the object load for `tdz_var` elides the hole check through the enclosing `BuildOptionalChain` hole check elision scope, allowing TheHole to leak. The fix moves `HoleCheckElisionScope` into `OptionalChainNullLabelScope` as a member, so it is correctly scoped and does not elide checks for the chain's base object loaded in outer contexts.
findings.suggestion: Move `HoleCheckElisionScope` from `BuildOptionalChain` into `OptionalChainNullLabelScope` as a member field initialized in the constructor. This restricts hole check elision to within the optional chain link scope (where dominance is guaranteed), rather than spanning the entire `BuildOptionalChain` call including its expression_func invocation. This prevents elision of hole checks for TDZ variables that serve as the base of an optional chain.

ground_truth.root_cause: The TDZ hole check elision optimization (`ignition_elide_redundant_tdz_checks`) added in `da0bcffa3d` placed `HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this)` at the start of `BuildOptionalChain`, covering the invocation of `expression_func()`. This function callback visits the actual chain expression, which may include TDZ variable accesses. The elision scope incorrectly treats all hole checks within the chain expression as redundant and suppresses them. The underlying assumption — that links 'earlier in the chain dominate later links' — applies to consecutive links of the same optional chain, but it incorrectly extends to the base object access itself, which is NOT dominated by any prior hole check.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 5666bca708c0 on top of intro 36f07e9a0448 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): RegExpMatchGlobalAtom_OneCharPattern in V8's regexp runtime uses SIMD (via Highway) to scan a subject string for occurrences of a single-character atom pattern, processing the bulk of the string in vector-width blocks and then falling back to a scalar loop for any trailing characters that don't fill a full SIMD lane. The scalar tail loop was written as `for (SChar c = *block; block < end; c = *(++block))`, which unconditionally reads `*block` in the for-loop initializer before the `block < end` bound check is performed. When the SIMD loops consume the subject string exactly to its end (leaving zero remaining scalar characters), `block` already equals `end`, and this initializer read accesses one character past the end of the allocated string buffer -- an out-of-bounds read. Root cause: The scalar cleanup loop's for-statement puts a pointer dereference in the initializer clause, which is unconditionally evaluated once before the loop's controlling condition is checked. This violates the invariant that `block` must be checked against `end` before every dereference, allowing a read exactly at (one past) the end of the subject string's backing buffer when there are no trailing characters left to scan.

findings.message: In the scalar 'remaining characters' tail loop of RegExpMatchGlobalAtom_OneCharPattern, the loop is written as a C-style for loop where the initializer unconditionally dereferences `*block` before the loop condition `block < end` is evaluated: `for (SChar c = *block; block < end; c = *(++block))`. Because the initializer executes exactly once regardless of the loop condition, when the preceding SIMD block-processing loops have already advanced `block` to equal `end` (i.e., there are zero remaining scalar characters to process), this initializer still performs `*block`, reading one character past the end of the allocated subject string buffer. Although the loaded value is discarded (the loop body never executes since `block < end` is false), the read itself is undefined behavior and can be flagged by ASan/MSan or crash on the last page of a mapped buffer, constituting an out-of-bounds read vulnerability.
findings.suggestion: Do not dereference `*block` in the loop initializer before verifying `block < end`. Restructure the loop so the character is only loaded after the bounds check, e.g. move the load inside the loop body: `for (; block < end; ++block) { SChar c = *block; ... }`. This guarantees the pointer is never dereferenced once it has reached `end`.

agent_reasoning: Without the added check, GetCycleRoot(isolate) is invoked unconditionally on every async parent module during ancestor gathering. GetCycleRoot() casts the module's cycle_root field directly to a SourceTextModule handle. For a parent module that fails synchronously while depending on an async child, cycle_root is never assigned and remains the uninitialized hole value. Calling ->status() on that casted hole treats the Hole oddball as if it were a SourceTextModule object, reading a 'status' field at an offset into memory that isn't actually a module object header — a type confusion that can leak or corrupt memory. The fix guards the call with `!IsTheHole(m->cycle_root(), isolate)` so GetCycleRoot() is only dereferenced when cycle_root has actually been initialized, eliminating the type confusion while preserving the original intent of the spec-derived check.

findings.message: In SourceTextModule::GatherAvailableAncestors, the loop over async parent modules evaluates `m->GetCycleRoot(isolate)->status() != kErrored` as the FIRST operand of the `&&`, meaning it is evaluated unconditionally for every async parent `m`, before checking whether `m` is already present in `exec_list`. GetCycleRoot() reads the module's `cycle_root` Tagged field and casts/dereferences it as a SourceTextModule (via Cast<SourceTextModule>). However, `cycle_root` is only guaranteed to be initialized (set to something other than the_hole) once a module has gone through specific points of the evaluation state machine. There is a scenario — an async parent module that depends on an async child but which itself fails synchronously before its cycle_root is ever assigned — where `cycle_root` remains the_hole when this function later runs (triggered when the async child eventually completes and walks up to gather available ancestors). Calling GetCycleRoot(isolate) in that state casts the Hole object to a SourceTextModule handle and then dereferences `->status()` on it, which is a type confusion / hole leak: the hole value is treated as a valid HeapObject of type SourceTextModule, and arbitrary offset reads are performed against it. Before this commit, the exec_list membership check was evaluated first, which happened to short-circuit away many calls to GetCycleRoot() on modules whose cycle_root had not been set; reordering the && operands here made the GetCycleRoot() call happen unconditionally on every iteration, which is a prerequisite for hitting the unguarded hole case that the later fix addresses.
findings.suggestion: Before calling GetCycleRoot(isolate) on m, explicitly check that m->cycle_root() is not the_hole (i.e. that CycleRoot has actually been initialized for this module). Only call GetCycleRoot()->status() once that is confirmed; otherwise treat the module as not having an errored cycle root for the purposes of this check (matching the later upstream fix, which adds `!IsTheHole(m->cycle_root(), isolate) &&` as the first conjunct and a DCHECK that cycle_root is only the_hole when m->status() == kErrored).

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix e194d3a40d8e on top of intro b9068d13bb1c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): V8's WebAssembly implementation stores per-module function signatures (and related C++ fast-API call signatures added during instantiation) in a `WasmModuleSignatureStorage` object held as a `mutable` field on the otherwise-const `WasmModule` struct. This storage can be appended to concurrently during module instantiation on one thread while another thread (e.g. performing `performance.measureMemory()` / memory-consumption tracing) reads its size via `WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize()` / `EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()`. The code that mutates `signature_storage` is correctly protected by `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_`, but the code that reads it for memory estimation purposes was not holding that same mutex, creating a data race on the underlying vector-of-vectors storage. Root cause: When `signature_zone` (a Zone) was replaced by the custom `WasmModuleSignatureStorage` class in commit b9068d13bb1, the new class's `TotalReservedSize()` accessor was invoked from `WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize()`/`EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` exactly as the old Zone accessor had been — i.e., without any synchronization — even though the class's own doc comment states that `signature_storage` is mutated during instantiation on a `const WasmModule`. The call chain `NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` → `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` executes before `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_` is acquired in that function, so a concurrent instantiation thread appending to `signature_storage` races with the reading thread.
commit_message:
[wasm] Introduce WasmModuleSignatureStorage

This replaces a Zone we used for storing signatures, array types, and
struct types. Zones are meant for temporary storage and are not very
memory efficient.

The new WasmModuleSignatureStorage provides pointer stability and a
similar interface than a zone, but has less memory overhead.
