findings.message: WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize() reads `signature_storage.TotalReservedSize()` (and the aggregate `WasmModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` which calls EstimateStoredSize()) without acquiring any lock. However, `signature_storage` (introduced in this commit, replacing the former `signature_zone`) is `mutable` and is concurrently mutated during instantiation (e.g. when fast API call signatures are added) while protected by `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_` elsewhere in the codebase. `NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` in wasm-code-manager.cc calls `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` at the very top of the function, before acquiring `allocation_mutex_` (the mutex is only taken later, around the `owned_code_`/`new_owned_code_`/`debug_info_` bookkeeping). Because the memory-consumption estimation can run concurrently (e.g. from `d8`'s performance.measureMemory or background profiling) with module instantiation on another thread that appends to `signature_storage`, this is a data race (TOCTOU/missing synchronization) on the underlying `std::vector<std::vector<uint8_t>> storage_` backing store, which can corrupt the vector's internal size/capacity bookkeeping or allow a torn read, leading to incorrect memory accounting and, under race conditions on reallocation, potential use of stale/invalid pointers or crashes. The original Zone-based implementation (`signature_zone.allocation_size_for_tracing()`) had the same unprotected access pattern, but the comment on the class explicitly acknowledges concurrent mutation during instantiation is expected, making the omission of locking in the size-estimation path a clear oversight.
findings.suggestion: Protect all accesses to `signature_storage` (both reads from EstimateStoredSize/EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption and writes during instantiation) with `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_`. In NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption(), acquire the allocation_mutex_ before calling `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` (which transitively reads signature_storage), and only release it after that call completes but before calling into `debug_info_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` to avoid a lock-order inversion with WasmScript::SetBreakPointForFunction. Also move `signature_storage.TotalReservedSize()` out of EstimateStoredSize() into EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption() so it is always evaluated under the lock.

findings.message: Shell::ResetOnProfileEndListener(Isolate*) is responsible for tearing down the per-isolate profiler-end callback state before an Isolate is disposed. The function was modified to add an early 'if (options.enable_inspector) return;' guard BEFORE the call to profiler_end_callback_.erase(isolate). When the inspector is enabled, the function returns immediately without erasing the isolate's entry from the profiler_end_callback_ map (which stores v8::Global<Function>/v8::Global<Context> handles keyed by Isolate*). Callers of ResetOnProfileEndListener (e.g. SourceGroup::ExecuteInThread, Worker::ExecuteInThread, Shell::Main, Shell::QuitOnce) call this function immediately before disposing the Isolate, expecting all isolate-associated state to be cleaned up. Because the erase is skipped whenever the inspector is enabled, the stale map entry (and the dangling Isolate* key, plus Global handles bound to a soon-to-be-destroyed Isolate) survives isolate disposal. Any later interaction that touches profiler_end_callback_ with the freed Isolate pointer (e.g. HasOnProfileEndListener/TriggerOnProfileEndListener being invoked again, e.g. if the isolate address is reused or the map is iterated/looked up) results in a use-after-free, since the stored Global<Function>/Global<Context> objects reference memory owned by the disposed isolate.
findings.suggestion: Perform the profiler_end_callback_.erase(isolate) call unconditionally, before checking options.enable_inspector, so the per-isolate map entry is always cleaned up regardless of whether the inspector console (D8Console) is installed. Only the D8Console-specific cleanup (console_delegate cast and DisposeProfiler()) should be skipped when the inspector is enabled.

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added an optimization in BuildCheckSmi that skips the runtime Smi check when TryGetInt32Constant proves the value lies in Smi range, without considering whether the input's value representation is tagged. For non-tagged representations this is safe because the fallback switch performs an equivalent value-range check. For tagged inputs, the fallback check (CheckSmi) verifies pointer tag bits rather than numeric value, and TryGetInt32Constant can return a value derived from a HeapNumber constant recorded via numeric-equality reasoning (CheckFloat64SameValue), not tag-verified equality. This mismatch allows the compiler to elide a necessary tag check, causing type confusion between Smi and HeapNumber, and a corresponding missing GC write barrier downstream. The fix restricts the elision to non-tagged value representations only, matching the upstream fix commit exactly, with no test files modified.
commit_message:
[maglev] Improve constant handling for BuildCheckSmi and the Array ctor

This patch improves the handling of constants in two places in the
Maglev graph builder:

1. In `BuildCheckSmi`: We can now often avoid emitting a runtime smi
check if the input is a constant that is known to be a smi at compile
time.
2. In `TryReduceConstructArrayConstructor`: When determining the
elements kind for a newly constructed array, we can now extract type
information from constant arguments even if they don't have a precise
NodeType set. This allows for more accurate elements kind selection.

These changes should lead to slightly better code generation in cases
involving constants.

fix_commit_message:
[maglev] Restrict BuildCheckSmi constant elision to non-tagged inputs

The elision added in CL 6988172 (commit 6469250a124a) skipped the
runtime check whenever TryGetInt32Constant(object) returned a value in
Smi range. For non-tagged input representations this is sound, because
the switch below emits a value-range check (CheckInt32IsSmi /
CheckUint32IsSmi / CheckFloat64IsSmi / CheckHoleyFloat64IsSmi /
CheckIntPtrIsSmi), which is exactly what Smi::IsValid proves.

For kTagged inputs the emitted check is CheckSmi, a tag-bit check.
Value-equivalence does not imply Smi tagging: a tagged node can be equal
in value to a Smi-range constant while actually holding a HeapNumber at
runtime. This happens when BuildCheckNumericalValue's HeapNumber branch
records a Constant(HeapNumber N) in the node's checked_value alternative
after a CheckFloat64SameValue; since CheckFloat64SameValue only proves
numeric equality, both Smi(N) and HeapNumber(N) pass it.
TryGetInt32Constant recurses through the alternative and returns N, so
the elision drops the tag check and a HeapNumber pointer can flow into
downstream consumers (e.g. the kSmi-field store path via
StoreTaggedFieldNoWriteBarrier), causing a type confusion and a missing
write barrier.

Gate the elision on value_representation() != kTagged. For tagged Smi
inputs the earlier StaticTypeIs(kSmi) / EnsureType(kSmi) early returns
already handle elision via type-system facts, which carry the tag
guarantee the value-equivalence alternative does not.

findings.message:
MaglevGraphBuilder::BuildCheckSmi() added an optimization that skips emitting the runtime Smi check whenever TryGetInt32Constant(object) returns a value that lies within the Smi range (Smi::IsValid). This is only sound when the emitted check would have been a value-range check (e.g. for kInt32/kUint32/kFloat64/kHoleyFloat64/kIntPtr inputs, where the subsequently-emitted CheckInt32IsSmi/CheckUint32IsSmi/CheckFloat64IsSmi/CheckHoleyFloat64IsSmi/CheckIntPtrIsSmi checks are exactly what Smi::IsValid proves).

However, for kTagged inputs the runtime check that would otherwise be emitted is CheckSmi, which is a tag-bit check, not a value-range check. TryGetInt32Constant() can recurse through a node's 'checked_value' alternative, which BuildCheckNumericalValue's HeapNumber branch can populate with a Constant(HeapNumber N) after only a CheckFloat64SameValue (a numeric-equality check that both a Smi(N) and a HeapNumber(N) satisfy). Consequently, for a kTagged node whose alternative records a HeapNumber constant with a value in Smi range, BuildCheckSmi incorrectly elides the CheckSmi tag check and returns the object as though it were proven to be a Smi.

This allows a HeapNumber pointer to flow into code paths that assume a Smi (e.g. field stores using StoreTaggedFieldNoWriteBarrier because the field is believed to hold only Smis), producing a type confusion and a missing write barrier - a serious, exploitable memory-safety bug reachable from JavaScript via Maglev-compiled code.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the constant-value-based elision to non-tagged input representations, since only those cases have the following switch emit an equivalent value-range check. For kTagged inputs, rely only on the earlier type-system checks (StaticTypeIs(kSmi) / EnsureType(kSmi)) which correctly carry the tag guarantee; do not elide the CheckSmi tag check based on value-equivalence alone.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 4e101ceb0b0b on top of intro 8d161a06cdbf via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): When --trace-deopt-verbose is enabled, Runtime_WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish in src/runtime/runtime-wasm.cc logs the wasm function being deoptimized by calling NativeModule::GetCode(). It passes a 'declared function index' (relative to the module's non-imported functions) into GetCode(), which expects a 'module function index' (including imported functions) and internally re-derives the declared index by subtracting num_imported_functions. This double conversion produces an incorrect (potentially negative) index used to access the NativeModule's code_table_ array, leading to an out-of-bounds read / DCHECK failure and an incorrect diagnostic function index/name being logged. Root cause: Two different kinds of wasm function indices exist in V8's codebase: the 'declared function index' (excludes imported functions) and the 'module function index' (includes imported functions). NativeModule::GetCode() expects the latter and performs its own conversion via declared_function_index(). The introducing commit passed the already-declared index directly to GetCode() without converting it back to a module-scoped index, causing the conversion to be applied twice.
commit_message:
[wasm][deoptimizer] Resolve feedback vector in WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish only

Previously the deoptimizer would try to lookup the feedback vector in
the vector of feedback vectors in the wasm trusted instance.
This was implemented at a time when I still assumed that there will
always be a valid feedback vector, however due to multi-instance
scenarios, this turned out to be incorrect. Later on this was fixed in
the WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish to allocate and fill in those feedback
vectors for which we didn't find one yet.

Moving the lookup of the feedback vector to the builtin exclusively
simplifies the code and also removes an access to the heap from within
the deoptimizer (which we'd ideally reduce down to zero if possible).

findings.message: In Runtime_WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish, when v8_flags.trace_deopt_verbose is enabled and a feedback vector needs to be allocated, the code calls trusted_instance_data->native_module()->GetCode(declared_func_index). However, declared_func_index is already the index relative to the first *declared* (non-imported) wasm function (it was decoded directly from the Smi stored in the liftoff frame's feedback-vector slot). NativeModule::GetCode(uint32_t index) expects a *module-scoped* function index (including imports) and internally converts it via declared_function_index(module(), index), which subtracts module->num_imported_functions again. Passing an already-declared index therefore causes a second, erroneous subtraction of num_imported_functions, producing a negative or otherwise wrong index used to access code_table_[...]. In debug builds this trips the DCHECK_LE/DCHECK_GT assertions inside declared_function_index(); in release builds (where DCHECKs are compiled out) it results in an out-of-bounds read into the NativeModule's code_table_ vector, which can crash the process or leak adjacent heap memory contents through code->DebugName() in the trace output. The same wrong index is also printed in the PrintF diagnostic message, misreporting the actual function.
findings.suggestion: Convert declared_func_index into a module-scoped function index before calling GetCode(), matching the convention used elsewhere (e.g. int module_func_index = trusted_instance_data->native_module()->num_imported_functions() + declared_func_index;), and use that value both for GetCode() and for the printed index.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 604e1bec5911 on top of intro 8a41470735aa via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): In V8's Maglev compiler, MaglevGraphBuilder::TryInferApiHolderValue() attempts to statically infer the 'holder' object for an API function call based on known receiver map information. As part of this, it calls MapInference::InsertMapChecks(), which can internally decide that graph building must abort (nulling out the builder's current basic block, e.g. current_block_) if it cannot safely insert the required map-check nodes. However, TryInferApiHolderValue() only had a single return type (compiler::HolderLookupResult) and mapped both the abort case and the legitimate 'holder could not be inferred' case to the same 'not_found' sentinel value. Its caller, TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction(), used this sentinel to decide to fall through and build a generic CallBuiltin node, unaware that graph building had actually aborted. This caused further IR nodes (including exception handler attachment via AttachExceptionHandlerInfo) to be emitted against an invalid/null current_block_, leading to a null-pointer dereference and crash. Root cause: Conflating two semantically distinct outcomes ('holder not found' vs 'graph building aborted') into a single sentinel return value, so the caller cannot detect that the compiler has entered a dead/aborted state and must stop emitting nodes.
commit_message:
[maglev] Introduce MapInference

This CL introduces `MapInference`, similar to TurboFan, to manage map
knowledge in Maglev.  Instead of clearing possible maps on side effects,
we now mark them as stale. This allows us to either ignore them or
re-verify them using `CheckMaps`.

All previous users of NodeInfo::possible_maps were updated to use the
MapInference interface; in addition to fetching the set of possible
maps, they are now required to call InsertMapChecks once the decision
has been made to use possible_maps.

InsertMapChecks only emits map checks when needed, ie when at least one
stale unstable map exists. Unreliable maps are "stale" when a side
effect may have occurred after we've last recorded them.

The --maglev-use-unreliable-maps flag, on by default, currently controls
whether Maglev uses stale unreliable maps by default, ie when no
explicit variant is passed to MapInference methods. Note that there is
no guarantee that *not* enabling this flag is identical to previous
behavior, since map tracking changed underneath (it should be similar
though). This flag is likely to be removed soon.

This CL also introduces KNA tracing: --trace-maglev-kna.

fix_commit_message:
[maglev] Don't swallow aborts in TryInferApiHolderValue

InsertMapChecks can abort (and null current_block_), but we'd
return the default "not found" sentinel, causing the caller in
TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction to fall through and emit a
CallBuiltin into a dead block. AttachExceptionHandlerInfo then
dereferences current_block_ and crashes.

Return std::optional instead; nullopt means the caller must
propagate DoneWithAbort.

findings.message: TryInferApiHolderValue() returns a plain compiler::HolderLookupResult. When inference.InsertMapChecks(zone()) detects that graph building has aborted (e.g. because a required map check could not be safely inserted and the current basic block was terminated/nulled), the function collapses this distinct 'abort' condition into the same 'not_found' sentinel value that it also returns for the ordinary, non-abort 'holder could not be inferred' case. The caller, MaglevGraphBuilder::TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction, cannot distinguish these two cases: it simply assigns the return value to api_holder and continues normal control flow via the switch on api_holder.lookup, falling through to emit further graph nodes (a CallBuiltin) into what is actually a dead/aborted block. AttachExceptionHandlerInfo (and other downstream code that assumes current_block_ is valid) then dereferences the now-null/invalid current_block_, causing a crash. This was introduced when MapInference was added and InsertMapChecks (which can internally abort graph building) was called with its abort result discarded/mapped to the ordinary not-found path.
findings.suggestion: Change TryInferApiHolderValue's return type to std::optional<compiler::HolderLookupResult> (or otherwise separately signal the abort condition) so that when InsertMapChecks aborts, the function returns std::nullopt instead of the same sentinel used for ordinary 'not found'. The caller (TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction) must check for this and immediately propagate ReduceResult::DoneWithAbort() instead of falling through to build further nodes in the now-dead block.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 63226679f9f5 on top of intro 551ade488094 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): While refactoring MaglevGraphBuilder::CanInlineCall into a shared MaglevReducer<BaseT>::CanInlineCall template (used by both the maglev builder and turbolev), the recursion-detection check was changed to consult MaglevReducer::current_provenance().unit — data that is sourced from the MaglevGraphLabeller, a component that is only actively maintained when GDB JIT interface support / tracing (--gdbjit, ENABLE_GDB_JIT_INTERFACE) is enabled. In release/non-tracing builds this provenance's `unit` pointer can be null. Calling `->shared_function_info()` on it during non-eager function inlining dereferences a null pointer and crashes the process (SIGSEGV). Additionally, because the graph labeller bookkeeping was being unconditionally performed for this data (regardless of whether gdbjit/tracing was enabled), it caused a related performance regression, which the fix commit also addresses by gating maglev_gdbjit metadata collection behind the actual gdbjit/tracing flags. Root cause: The direct-recursion self-inlining check was changed from reading the builder's own always-valid MaglevCompilationUnit pointer to instead reading MaglevGraphLabeller-derived provenance data, which is only guaranteed to be populated when GDB JIT interface support or graph tracing is active. This coupled a functional correctness check to an optional, debug-only subsystem, producing a null-pointer dereference when that subsystem was disabled (the common release-build case).

fix_commit_message:
[maglev] Disable maglev_gdbjit without gdbjit

Without ENABLE_GDB_JIT_INTERFACE or --gdbjit the maglev metadata
collection should be disabled.

Fixes performance regressions from uselessly recording the data.
Also fixes a SIGSEGV crash during non-eager inlining where the
direct recursion check relied on the debug-only graph labeller's
provenance mapping (which is null in release/non-tracing builds).

findings.message: When MaglevGraphBuilder::CanInlineCall was moved/refactored into the shared MaglevReducer<BaseT>::CanInlineCall template, the direct-recursion self-inlining guard was rewritten from comparing against the builder's own `compilation_unit_->shared_function_info()` to instead reading `current_provenance().unit->shared_function_info()`. `current_provenance()` returns the MaglevGraphLabeller::Provenance record that is only populated/valid when a graph labeller is present and actively tracking node provenance (i.e. under ENABLE_GDB_JIT_INTERFACE / --gdbjit or tracing flags). In ordinary release builds / non-tracing configurations the `unit` field of the current provenance can be null, so dereferencing `current_provenance().unit->shared_function_info()` during non-eager inlining causes a SIGSEGV (null pointer dereference) instead of safely evaluating the recursion check against the always-valid current compilation unit.
findings.suggestion: Do not rely on the debug/tracing-only MaglevGraphLabeller provenance data for correctness-relevant logic such as the direct-recursion check. Pass the caller's actual MaglevCompilationUnit explicitly into CanInlineCall (as the fix does: `CanInlineCall(const MaglevCompilationUnit* current_unit, ...)`), guard the pointer with a null check, and compare against that explicit unit instead of `current_provenance().unit`.
findings.title: Null pointer dereference in MaglevReducer::CanInlineCall direct-recursion check

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Null pointer dereference in MaglevReducer::CanInlineCall direct-recursion check

ground_truth.root_cause: The direct-recursion self-inlining check was changed from reading the builder's own always-valid MaglevCompilationUnit pointer to instead reading MaglevGraphLabeller-derived provenance data, which is only guaranteed to be populated when GDB JIT interface support or graph tracing is active. This coupled a functional correctness check to an optional, debug-only subsystem, producing a null-pointer dereference when that subsystem was disabled (the common release-build case).
